stories.title: Handcream made to perfection, a read
Built like it still has a train to catch

Galli.dek: Hand-worked shine, worn the way the lanes wear it: loud, easy and a little bit regal.
Galli.lede: Galli means lane, and this shoot never leaves one: shop signs overhead, a rickshaw for a throne, and a look that turns the street into a runway.
blocks: A beaded cropped jacket meets wide dark denim and glossy platform loafers, then gets piled with heirloom-style jewellery: layered chokers, a long pendant chain, rings on every other finger.
The bag does the talking: a sequinned top-handle, held as casually as a grocery tote. It is the kind of styling that makes old-world craft feel like today.

Gully Labs.dek: A sneaker label that still believes the best tool in the workshop is a pair of hands.
Gully Labs.lede: Walk into the workshop and the first thing you notice is the sound: not machines, but the soft pull of thread through suede, again and again, until it becomes a rhythm.
blocks: Every pair starts as a flat sheet of leather and a chalk outline. From there it is cut, skived, punched and stitched — slowly, deliberately, by people who have done this long enough that their hands move before they think.

The designs borrow from the street: court shoes, runners, the beaten-in trainers you see on every corner. But the finish is closer to a tailor’s than a factory’s. Edges are burnished. Stitch lines are straight enough to rule a page.
Suede, cut and finished by hand before it ever meets a sole.
Handwork means fewer pairs. It also means each one carries small differences — a stitch that sits a millimetre left, a panel with a deeper nap. The studio calls those signatures, not flaws.
If a machine can make it perfect, we’d rather make it personal.
It is a slower way to build a shoe, and a quieter way to sell one. No hype drops, no countdowns — just a pair that gets better the longer you wear it.
Low-tops, finished in the studio’s signature suede.

Cord.dek: On belts, buckles and the small finishing touch that pulls an outfit into shape.
Cord.lede: Some pieces shout. Cord’s pieces hold things together — literally. A cinched waist, a knotted strap, a belt that turns a loose shape into a silhouette.
blocks: The label works in earthy, sun-faded colours: rust, mustard, clay, tobacco. Fabrics are soft enough to drape and sturdy enough to keep their line through a long day.
A belted coat, worn loose until the buckle decides otherwise.
Look closely and most designs hinge on one detail — a tie, a strap, a fastening placed exactly where your eye lands. Take it away and the piece is fine. Leave it in and the whole outfit clicks.
Style is mostly a question of where you pull the string.
Wear it with denim on a weekday, with heels on a weekend, or with nothing but confidence and a good pair of sunglasses.
Knits in the label’s sun-washed palette.

Project Qaafi.dek: A hand cream in an aluminium tube, and the case for making one small thing very well.
Project Qaafi.lede: It comes in a crimped metal tube that dents a little more every time you use it. That is the point: an object that records your days, the way a good leather bag does.
blocks: Project Qaafi makes very few things, and it treats each one like a flagship. The hand cream is rich without being greasy, absorbs fast, and leaves a scent that is closer to a memory than a perfume.
Each blend is built around notes you would recognise from home — warm wood, something smoky, something green. It is meant to be noticed by you, not announced to a room.
We wanted something you reach for without thinking, and miss when it runs out.
Pocket it, keep it by the desk, leave it by the door. The tube will tell you how often you did.

Nappa Dori.dek: Trunks, bags and travel goods built with the old-world romance of a railway platform.
Nappa Dori.lede: There is a particular kind of luggage that belongs on a station platform at dawn: hard-cornered, brass-latched, carried by someone who knows exactly where they are going.
blocks: Nappa Dori’s pieces borrow that romance and make it practical. Structured trunks sit alongside soft weekenders, everyday backpacks and the kind of wallet that gets better with every year in a back pocket.
Leather that softens and darkens with use.
Hardware is chunky and honest. Leather is chosen to age rather than stay pristine. The design language is part heritage, part city — as at home on an airport carousel as on a commuter train.
A good bag should look better at the end of the trip than at the start.
Pack light, pack heavy, pack in a hurry. These are built for all three.
Finishing details, made to be handled.

Doodlage.dek: Fashion made from what the industry throws away — and made to look like it never did.
Doodlage.lede: Every season, the fashion business leaves behind mountains of offcuts and surplus fabric. Doodlage starts there, and works backwards towards something beautiful.
blocks: Panels are pieced together from leftover rolls, so no two garments are quite alike. The patchwork is the design, not a disguise.
Small batches, pieced from surplus fabric.
The label keeps runs small, reuses what it can, and designs pieces meant to stay in a wardrobe for years rather than a season.
The most sustainable garment is the one you keep wearing.
Easy shirts, cut from rescued cotton.
It is fashion with a conscience that never asks you to sacrifice the fun part.
